successors.name: South African Republic (Transvaal)
successors.text: Sekhukhuneland: 'In about 1650, they settled in the area to the south of the Steelpoort River'

capitals.name: Manganeng on the Steelpoort River (stand-in inside Sekhukhuneland)
Phiring, then Thaba Mosego (stand-in inside Sekhukhuneland)

ledger.x: c. 1780: the Maroteng Pedi state stands under King Thulare. 'Towards the end of the 18th century, the primary Pedi state was established, led by supreme leaders from the Maroteng clan'; Thulare (c. 1780-1820) held land 'from present-day Rustenburg ... to the lowveld ... as far south as the Vaal River'.

c. 1826: Thulare's outer lands are lost in the Mfecane. Sekwati page: 'Around 1826, the Ndebele under Mzilikazi seized the opportunity and overthrew the Pedi regime', killing several of Thulare's sons; Swazi campaigns against the Pedi 'failed to take their mountain strongholds' (undated). The Pedi people page names…
May 1876: the South African Republic goes to war with Sekhukhune.
April 1877: the British annex the Transvaal, ending the Boer war against the Pedi.
1879: the British under Wolseley attack Sekhukhune.
1879: Sekhukhune is defeated and imprisoned in Pretoria ('defeated him in 1879'; 'imprisoned in Pretoria, but later released after the first South African War').
1882: Sekhukhune is assassinated and the monarchy dismantled.

wars.name: Pedi wars with the Transvaal, the Swazi and Britain
wars.outcome: 'From 1876 to 1879, the Pedi engaged in wars with the Boers and the British, resulting in defeat and the Pedi state falling under Boer influence'; the Transvaal declared war in May 1876; the British annexed the Transvaal in April 1877 and defeated Sekhukhune…

certainty.note: No frontier is described; the Pedi polity was a paramountcy of the Maroteng over tributary chiefdoms.
